items.prompt: What does this unit mean by a "design pattern"?
choices: A block of code you copy-paste directly into your project
A named, reusable shape for solving a recurring structural problem — a vocabulary word, not a mandate
A required checklist every senior engineer must follow
A synonym for "object-oriented programming"
items.explanation: A design pattern is a named shape for a recurring problem, useful as shared vocabulary between engineers. It's not a literal snippet to paste, and using one is never mandatory just because it exists.
items.reference:
🏷️ Design pattern — a named, reusable shape for a recurring structural problem
📚 Not a mandate, not code to copy-paste verbatim
📖 GoF catalog: Creational / Structural / Behavioral

items.prompt: What does "cargo-culting" mean in this unit's usage?
choices: Reproducing the visible shape of a practice without the conditions that made it useful
Writing code without any tests
Using outdated programming languages
Copying code from Stack Overflow
items.explanation: Cargo-culting means reproducing a practice's surface form (e.g. a pattern's classes/interfaces) while missing the actual problem-condition that made the practice valuable in its original context.
items.reference:
🛬 Cargo-culting — copying a practice's visible shape without the conditions that made it work
📄 Résumé-driven design — choosing a solution for how it looks on paper
items.learnMore: The term comes from Pacific islanders who, having seen WWII cargo planes land near airstrips, built runway-shaped structures out of straw hoping planes would land again — they reproduced the visible shape without the radio infrastructure, supply chains, and military logistics that actually caused the landings. In code, adding a Strategy pattern because a competitor's blog post used one reproduces the shape (interfaces, classes, a factory) without reproducing the condition that made it worth it there (real, independently-varying implementations).

items.prompt: "Résumé-driven design" refers to:
choices: Choosing a solution because it looks good on paper, not because the problem needs it
Designing software based on a hiring manager's job posting
A specific pattern for organizing a résumé document
Refactoring code right before a performance review
items.explanation: Résumé-driven design is choosing a pattern or technology for how it reads (impressive, modern, "best practice") rather than because the actual problem in front of you calls for it.

items.prompt: Sam's shipping calculator has 2 branches added in the same PR, with no plan to diverge. According to L1, what does this suggest about Priya's Strategy-pattern suggestion?
choices: It's a bad pattern in general and should never be used
The pattern's cost would be paid without a real problem to fix — this isn't Strategy's problem here
It's correct because any conditional logic should use a pattern
It's correct because Priya is more senior than Sam
items.explanation: L1's point isn't that Strategy is bad — it's that this specific code doesn't have the problem Strategy solves, so every cost of adopting it (extra files, extra indirection) is paid for nothing.
items.reference:
🧾 Shipping calculator — 2 branches, added in the same PR
📈 No plan for a third region, no runtime swap needed
💬 Priya's comment: "conditional logic → use a pattern"
items.learnMore: The shipping calculator's if/else has conditional logic — but so does almost every function anywhere. "Has conditional logic" filters nothing. What actually matters, developed fully in L2, is whether the branches vary independently and whether the direct version is already causing a measurable cost — neither is true here, which is why the pattern would be pure overhead with nothing to show for it.

items.prompt: What is the strongest evidence, from L1, that the Strategy-pattern rewrite of the shipping calculator was overkill?
choices: It replaced 6 lines of stable logic with 4 types that produce the exact same behavior, with nothing to swap and nothing new to test

Priya is not a shipping-domain expert
The original if/else was written by a junior engineer
items.explanation: The rewrite added an interface, two classes, and a factory to reproduce behavior a single lookup could express in one line — no runtime swapping, no new testability gained, just more surface area for the same answer.

items.prompt: Which of these is listed in L1 as a real cost of adding a pattern?
choices: More files/types, more indirection, slower onboarding for new readers
Patterns always make code run slower at runtime
Patterns are against most style guides
Patterns increase the number of production bugs by definition
items.explanation: L1's cost table lists more files/types, more indirection, slower onboarding, and premature abstraction — all real, structural costs, not claims about runtime speed or bug counts.
items.reference:
📁 More files/types
🔀 More indirection
🐢 Slower onboarding
🔮 Premature abstraction
items.learnMore: Indirection isn't free even when the pattern is "correct" — following the logic now means jumping through an extra layer (interface → concrete class → factory) no matter who's reading it or why. That cost is paid on every read, by every future engineer, regardless of whether the flexibility gained (the ability to swap implementations) is ever actually used. A pattern only nets positive when the flexibility gets used often enough to outweigh that constant reading tax.

Because indirect code always produces more runtime errors
Because indirection doubles the CPU cost of every function call
items.explanation: The reading cost of an extra layer is paid by every future reader on every read — it doesn't matter whether the pattern is theoretically the "right" one if that flexibility is never exercised in practice.

items.prompt: True or false: a design pattern is code you copy-paste verbatim into a new project.
choices: True — that's the whole point of a pattern
False — a pattern is a reusable shape/vocabulary; the actual code differs per use case
True, but only for Creational patterns
False — patterns only apply to functional languages
items.explanation: A pattern names a shape (an interface plus interchangeable implementations, for Strategy) — the actual types, method names, and logic are written fresh for each real problem.
items.reference:
🏷️ Pattern = vocabulary, not a literal snippet
🗣️ "Just make it a Strategy" replaces a whole re-explanation
items.learnMore: Two engineers who both know the Strategy pattern can communicate an entire design in four words ("just make it a Strategy") instead of re-deriving the interface-plus-implementations shape from scratch in conversation. That's the actual value of the vocabulary — it's a compression tool for talking about code, not a template to stamp onto every problem with conditional logic.

items.prompt: At a glance, what problem does the Strategy pattern solve?
choices: Swapping an algorithm/behavior at runtime among interchangeable implementations
Guaranteeing exactly one instance of a class
Adding responsibilities to an object dynamically
Reconciling two incompatible interfaces
items.explanation: Strategy lets you select among interchangeable implementations of a behavior, typically at runtime — the other three descriptions belong to Singleton, Decorator, and Adapter respectively.
items.reference:
✅ Good sign — ≥2 variants, chosen at runtime, growing
🚫 Bad sign — 1-2 branches, stable, decided at compile time
items.learnMore: Strategy's whole reason to exist is swapping an algorithm/behavior at runtime among interchangeable implementations. When there's nothing to swap at runtime and only one or two variants that never change independently, the pattern's machinery (interface, classes, factory) is reproducing behavior a single function or lookup already expressed — with none of the runtime flexibility the pattern is actually for.

items.prompt: Which of these is the "bad sign" this unit lists for Strategy being cargo-culted?
choices: 1-2 branches, never expected to grow, decided at compile time
Five real, growing variants added independently by different teams
A runtime configuration switch between implementations
Unit tests that isolate each variant
items.explanation: A stable 1-2-branch case decided once at compile time has no runtime swapping and no growth — exactly the opposite of what Strategy is for, which is the tell that it's being reached for out of habit, not need.

items.prompt: Implement `PaymentRegistry`: `register(name, strategy)` stores a strategy object under `name`; `resolve(name)` returns the stored strategy, or throws `new Error('No strategy for ' + name)` if nothing is registered under that name.

tests.description: register then resolve returns the same strategy
tests.expr: const r = new PaymentRegistry(); const s = { charge: () => 'ok' }; r.register('cc', s); expect(r.resolve('cc')).toBe(s);

tests.description: resolving an unregistered name throws
tests.expr: const r = new PaymentRegistry(); expect(() => r.resolve('crypto')).toThrow();

tests.description: two different names resolve to two different strategies
tests.expr: const r = new PaymentRegistry(); const a = { id: 'a' }; const b = { id: 'b' }; r.register('a', a); r.register('b', b); expect(r.resolve('a')).toBe(a); expect(r.resolve('b')).toBe(b);

items.explanation: A Map keyed by name is exactly the registry described in L3 — register() adds an entry, resolve() looks it up and fails loudly (not silently returning undefined) when nothing matches, so a typo'd processor name surfaces immediately instead of failing deep inside a charge attempt.
items.reference:
🗺️ A registry (Map) replaces a switch statement
➕ A new processor registers itself — no shared file edited
🧪 Each strategy is testable in isolation
items.learnMore: A switch statement on processor name has the same reading cost as the direct if/else it's meant to replace, and every new processor still means editing that one shared function — exactly the merge-conflict problem Strategy is supposed to fix. A registry keyed by name flips that: adding processor #6 means one new line, in whichever team's own file registers it, touching nothing anyone else owns. That's Q2 (independent variation) and Q4 (concrete gain) made literal in code, not just asserted in prose.

items.prompt: Implement `createPaymentRegistry()`, a factory returning an object with two methods sharing a private `Map` via closure: `register(name, fn)` and `resolve(name)` (throws `new Error('No strategy for ' + name)` if missing).

tests.description: register then resolve returns the same function
tests.expr: const r = createPaymentRegistry(); const fn = () => 'ok'; r.register('cc', fn); expect(r.resolve('cc')).toBe(fn);

tests.description: resolving an unregistered name throws
tests.expr: const r = createPaymentRegistry(); expect(() => r.resolve('crypto')).toThrow();

tests.description: two separate registries don't share state
tests.expr: const r1 = createPaymentRegistry(); const r2 = createPaymentRegistry(); r1.register('a', () => 1); expect(() => r2.resolve('a')).toThrow();

items.explanation: Closures give each registry its own private Map without a class — register/resolve share `strategies` through the closure, and a second call to the factory produces a completely independent registry, which the third test checks directly.

items.prompt: Implement `withRetry(fn, maxAttempts)` — returns a new function that calls `fn()`, and if it throws, retries (calling `fn()` again) up to `maxAttempts` total attempts before rethrowing the last error.

tests.description: succeeds immediately if fn never throws
tests.expr: let calls = 0; const fn = () => { calls++; return 'ok'; }; const wrapped = withRetry(fn, 3); expect(wrapped()).toBe('ok'); expect(calls).toBe(1);

tests.description: retries until success within maxAttempts
tests.expr: let calls = 0; const fn = () => { calls++; if (calls < 3) throw new Error('fail'); return 'ok'; }; const wrapped = withRetry(fn, 3); expect(wrapped()).toBe('ok'); expect(calls).toBe(3);

tests.description: rethrows after exhausting maxAttempts
tests.expr: let calls = 0; const fn = () => { calls++; throw new Error('always fails'); }; const wrapped = withRetry(fn, 2); expect(() => wrapped()).toThrow(); expect(calls).toBe(2);

items.explanation: This is the function-based version of L3's `RetryingPaymentStrategy` — same loop-and-catch shape, just wrapping a plain function instead of an object's method, which is what makes it composable with other function-based decorators like withLogging.
items.reference:
🎁 Each decorator wraps a function, returning a new function
🧵 Decorators compose — retry + logging, independently
items.learnMore: Each decorator here (`withRetry`, `withLogging`) takes a function and returns a new function with the same call signature plus one extra behavior — the caller can't tell the difference from the outside. That's what makes them combinable: `withLogging(withRetry(charge))` and `withRetry(withLogging(charge))` are both valid, and which order you pick determines whether logging sees the retried attempts or not (see L3's failure-modes table on stack order).

items.prompt: Implement `withLogging(fn, log)` — returns a new function that calls `fn(...args)`, passes the result to `log(result)`, then returns the result unchanged. `log` is an injected function so it can be replaced with a recorder in tests instead of printing to the console.

tests.description: returns fn's result unchanged
tests.expr: const wrapped = withLogging((x) => x * 2, () => {}); expect(wrapped(5)).toBe(10);

tests.description: calls log with the result
tests.expr: const logs = []; const wrapped = withLogging((x) => x * 2, (r) => logs.push(r)); wrapped(5); expect(logs).toEqual([10]);

tests.description: passes through multiple arguments to fn
tests.expr: const wrapped = withLogging((a, b) => a + b, () => {}); expect(wrapped(2, 3)).toBe(5);

items.explanation: Injecting `log` instead of hardcoding console.log is what makes this testable in isolation — exactly the Q4 payoff L2's checklist asks about, applied to a decorator instead of a Strategy.

items.prompt: Implement `compose2(outer, inner)` for combining two decorators shaped like `withRetry`/`withLogging` (each of shape `(fn) => wrappedFn`): return a single decorator function `(fn) => outer(inner(fn))`. This is what lets decorators like `LoggingPaymentStrategy`/`RetryingPaymentStrategy` combine without a class per combination.

tests.description: applies inner's wrapping before outer's, around the same call
tests.expr: const trace = []; const markA = (fn) => (...a) => { trace.push('A-before'); const r = fn(...a); trace.push('A-after'); return r; }; const markB = (fn) => (...a) => { trace.push('B-before'); const r = fn(...a); trace.push('B-after'); return r; }; const combined = compose2(markA, markB)((x) => { trace.push('core'); return x; }); combined(1); expect(trace).toEqual(['A-before', 'B-before', 'core', 'B-after', 'A-after']);

tests.description: identity decorators pass the return value through unchanged
tests.expr: const identity = (fn) => fn; const combined = compose2(identity, identity)((x) => x + 1); expect(combined(9)).toBe(10);

tests.description: outer wraps the entire inner+fn call, not just fn directly
tests.expr: const calls = []; const outer = (fn) => (x) => { calls.push('outer-start'); const r = fn(x); calls.push('outer-end'); return r; }; const inner = (fn) => (x) => { calls.push('inner-start'); const r = fn(x); calls.push('inner-end'); return r; }; const combined = compose2(outer, inner)((x) => { calls.push('core:' + x); return x * 2; }); expect(combined(5)).toBe(10); expect(calls).toEqual(['outer-start', 'inner-start', 'core:5', 'inner-end', 'outer-end']);

items.explanation: `outer(inner(fn))` wraps `inner`'s wrapping around `fn` first, then `outer`'s wrapping around that whole thing — matching L3's `Logging(Retrying(x))` ordering, where the outermost decorator is the last one to run on the way out and the first on the way in.

items.prompt: Implement `createLogger(level)`: for `level === 'verbose'`, return `{ level, log: (msg) => '[VERBOSE] ' + msg }`; for `level === 'quiet'`, return `{ level, log: (msg) => null }`; for any other value, throw `new Error('Unknown level: ' + level)`.

tests.description: verbose logger prefixes messages
tests.expr: const logger = createLogger('verbose'); expect(logger.log('hi')).toBe('[VERBOSE] hi');

tests.description: quiet logger returns null
tests.expr: const logger = createLogger('quiet'); expect(logger.log('hi')).toBe(null);

tests.description: unknown level throws
tests.expr: expect(() => createLogger('debug')).toThrow();

items.explanation: This is a real Factory Method case only if 'verbose' and 'quiet' genuinely need different behavior (one silences output, one doesn't) — which they do here, so the branching construction logic earns its place, unlike the next variant.

items.prompt: Implement a minimal Observer: `createEventBus()` returns `{ subscribe(fn), notify(data) }`. `subscribe(fn)` registers a listener. `notify(data)` calls every registered listener with `data`, in registration order.

tests.description: calls a single subscriber with the notified data
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const received = []; bus.subscribe((d) => received.push(d)); bus.notify('order-completed'); expect(received).toEqual(['order-completed']);

tests.description: calls multiple subscribers, in registration order
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const order = []; bus.subscribe(() => order.push('email')); bus.subscribe(() => order.push('fraud')); bus.notify('x'); expect(order).toEqual(['email', 'fraud']);

tests.description: a subscriber added after one notify still receives the next one
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const received = []; bus.subscribe(() => received.push('first')); bus.notify('a'); bus.subscribe(() => received.push('second')); bus.notify('b'); expect(received).toEqual(['first', 'first', 'second']);

items.explanation: An array of listener functions plus a loop in notify() is the entire mechanism — this is Observer's core shape stripped of any framework-specific event-emitter API.
items.reference:
📢 notify(data) — calls every subscribed listener
🔕 unsubscribe — removes one listener without affecting others
items.learnMore: The event bus never needs to know what email, fraud-scoring, or analytics do with an order-completed event — it just calls every subscribed listener with the data. That's Observer's whole value: the source and its listeners can be written, tested, and deployed by different teams without either side depending on the other's implementation.

items.prompt: Extend the Observer shape with unsubscribe: implement `createEventBus()` returning `{ subscribe(fn), notify(data) }` where `subscribe(fn)` returns an `unsubscribe` function that removes that specific listener when called.

tests.description: unsubscribe stops that listener from receiving future notifications
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const received = []; const unsub = bus.subscribe((d) => received.push(d)); bus.notify('a'); unsub(); bus.notify('b'); expect(received).toEqual(['a']);

tests.description: unsubscribing one listener doesn't affect others
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const received = []; const unsubA = bus.subscribe(() => received.push('A')); bus.subscribe(() => received.push('B')); unsubA(); bus.notify('x'); expect(received).toEqual(['B']);

tests.description: calling unsubscribe twice is safe and has no extra effect
tests.expr: const bus = createEventBus(); const received = []; const unsub = bus.subscribe(() => received.push('x')); unsub(); unsub(); bus.notify('y'); expect(received).toEqual([]);

items.explanation: Filtering by reference equality (`l !== fn`) removes exactly the one listener a given unsubscribe call closed over, and filtering (rather than splicing by index) makes a second call to the same unsubscribe function a safe no-op — the listener is already gone.

items.prompt: Widgetly's checkout expects every payment processor to expose `charge(amountCents)`. A legacy processor instead exposes `legacyPay(dollars, cents)`. Implement `adaptLegacyProcessor(legacy)` returning `{ charge(amountCents) }` that calls `legacy.legacyPay(dollars, cents)` with the amount split correctly (e.g. 1234 cents -> dollars 12, cents 34), returning whatever `legacyPay` returns.

tests.description: splits amountCents into dollars and cents correctly
tests.expr: let captured; const legacy = { legacyPay: (d, c) => { captured = [d, c]; return 'paid'; } }; const adapted = adaptLegacyProcessor(legacy); adapted.charge(1234); expect(captured).toEqual([12, 34]);

tests.description: returns the legacy call's result
tests.expr: const legacy = { legacyPay: () => 'legacy-ok' }; const adapted = adaptLegacyProcessor(legacy); expect(adapted.charge(500)).toBe('legacy-ok');

tests.description: handles an amount under 100 cents (0 whole dollars)
tests.expr: let captured; const legacy = { legacyPay: (d, c) => { captured = [d, c]; } }; adaptLegacyProcessor(legacy).charge(45); expect(captured).toEqual([0, 45]);

items.explanation: The adapter's whole job is the translation math (splitting cents into dollars+cents) plus forwarding the call — the legacy processor is untouched, and every other call site keeps using the one clean `charge(amountCents)` interface.

It's a bad sign when both interfaces being adapted between are ones you designed yourself — that usually means picking one shape and using it everywhere, not building a translation layer between two of your own inconsistent designs.

items.prompt: A different legacy processor exposes `pay({ amount, currency })`, where `amount` is a decimal number of whole currency units (dollars), not cents. Implement `adaptDecimalProcessor(legacy)` returning `{ charge(amountCents) }` that converts cents to a decimal dollar amount and calls `legacy.pay({ amount, currency: 'USD' })`, returning its result.

tests.description: converts cents to a decimal dollar amount
tests.expr: let captured; const legacy = { pay: (arg) => { captured = arg; return 'ok'; } }; adaptDecimalProcessor(legacy).charge(1250); expect(captured).toEqual({ amount: 12.5, currency: 'USD' });

tests.description: returns the legacy call's result
tests.expr: const legacy = { pay: () => 'decimal-ok' }; expect(adaptDecimalProcessor(legacy).charge(100)).toBe('decimal-ok');

tests.description: handles a whole-dollar amount with no remaining cents
tests.expr: let captured; const legacy = { pay: (arg) => { captured = arg; } }; adaptDecimalProcessor(legacy).charge(500); expect(captured).toEqual({ amount: 5, currency: 'USD' });

items.explanation: Two adapters for two differently-shaped legacy interfaces, both converging on the same `charge(amountCents)` contract — this is what lets the payment registry from earlier in L3 register legacy processors right alongside native ones, with no special-casing at the call site.
